A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TTS research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching v1 Appendix I to v2 Appendix H.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix I report original NQ and ClashEval experiments, source-scoring simulations, collusion tests, and model ablations.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix H report revised original experiments, retain the earlier model ablations, and add a case study using conflicting web evidence.

M1.justification: Sections 2.3 and 3.5 introduce A/B grouping: sources are scored on claims generated from the opposite group, replacing separate leave-one-out claim construction in the main experiments. This changes claim construction while retaining the peer-prediction score, threshold filtering, and final summarization.

E1.justification: NQ and ClashEval remain. Appendix H.5 adds 43 items from Open-Domain QA with Conflicting Contexts, extending evaluation to naturally occurring web evidence augmented with prompt injections and, when needed, a generated deceptive source. This is a limited extension within the existing summarization task.

E2.justification: The main comparisons retain Initial Synthesis, Majority Prompt, and Majority Claims; collusion experiments retain the all-sources baseline and majority-based scoring rule. The added web-evidence case uses the existing three main baselines. Newly discussed related methods are not evaluated.

E3.justification: The main evaluation expands from 300 queries per dataset to 1,299 ClashEval queries and approximately 1,100 NQ queries, with v2 inconsistently reporting 1,100 versus 1,131. ClashEval changes from balanced domain sampling to all unique queries with randomly selected mod_degree. The main experiments adopt A/B grouping and add a fourth faithful paraphrase, producing seven sources despite residual six-source wording. The web case adds filtering and attack-augmentation procedures.

E4.justification: Appendix H.5 adds a case study testing robustness on augmented web evidence and reports a label-quality audit flagging roughly 23% of labels. The collusion analysis is revised, with Table 5 adding a third truthful source despite unchanged two-source prose. Stance-flipping analysis and the three model-configuration ablations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or repeated-run and seed counts. The retained theoretical concentration bounds are not empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–6 and Figures 3–4 report revised main results. For example, TTS NQ precision and answer accuracy change from 81.0% and 70.7% to 76.1% and 72.3% under changed settings, not a comparable performance gain. New Table 7 reports 80.6% precision and 65.9% accuracy for the web case. Earlier 300-query results remain in Appendix H.9.

T1.justification: V1 Appendix H is removed, including Proposition 3, assumption A3′, and extensions of the guarantees to claim-dependent coverage, signal quality, and reporting for the scored source. The central proofs remain unchanged. V2 Section 3.5 adds an argument that A/B grouping preserves the guarantees and reduces complexity to O(K|C|).

C1.justification: The abstract, three contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about incentive-aligned source selection, truthfulness guarantees, and improved factuality and robustness. The expanded introduction explains the motivation without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix D substantially expands applicability and limitations: idealized assumptions, unique information, minority-versus-majority conflicts, reliance on external priors, and the static single-query scope. Appendix H.5 explains the synthetic evaluation's intended role and qualifies the web case through its small sample and noisy labels.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository link, a fourth faithful-source generation prompt, and implementation information for A/B grouping. Section 4.2 newly reports per-query input, output, and thinking-token usage and an estimated $0.07 cost. The existing pipeline and evaluation prompts are retained.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds computational mechanism design context, including RegretNet, GemNet, and LLM-based auction and preference-elicitation research. The conflicting-context dataset is also newly cited. These additions broaden the context while retaining the central positioning between RAG robustness and peer prediction.

P1.justification: V2 expands the introductory motivation, adds an accessible theoretical overview, compresses the framework steps into prose, and introduces a computational-complexity subsection. Appendix headings and numbering change, but most retained technical text, the abstract, and conclusion remain stable.

P2.justification: Figures 3 and 4 are redrawn with additional source categories and revised axes and labels. Two web-case tables are added, and main accuracy tables drop numerator/denominator counts while retaining their headers. Figures 1–2 and the overall document design remain essentially unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 modestly improves practical assessability through implementation and cost disclosures, a code link, expanded evaluation, and clearer limitations. These benefits are tempered by removal of the heterogeneity extension and new reporting inconsistencies. In particular, NQ counts disagree across sections, and Table 2 reports 56.1% F1 although its 86.2% precision and 31.5% recall imply approximately 46.1%, limiting confidence in the revised reporting.
